dataset.title: Fossil-fuel share of electricity generation (Ember via OWID)

indicator.name: Fossil share of generation
indicator.description: Share of electricity generated by fossil fuels: Electricity generation from coal, oil, and gas, measured as a percentage of total electricity produced in the country or region.

source.name: Our World in Data – Energy dataset (Ember electricity data)
source.license: CC BY 4.0 (Our World in Data; underlying Ember data CC BY 4.0)
source.citation: Ember – Yearly Electricity Data (2026); Ember – Yearly Electricity Data Europe (2026) – with major processing by Our World in Data. File owid_energy.csv downloaded from https://catalog.ourworldindata.org/energy/owid_energy/owid_energy.csv on 2026-10-12 19:10 UTC (server Last-Modified: Wed, 30 Sep 2026 14:42:02 GMT).

upstream.name: Ember – Yearly Electricity Data (2026) and Yearly Electricity Data Europe (2026)

notes: Imported from data/raw/owid/owid_energy.csv, column "fossil_fuels_electricity_share_pct", years 1990 on (one row per country and year; the latest year with a value is shown, the full series is kept for charts and derived datasets).

Codebook (data/raw/owid/owid_energy.codebook.csv) title: "Share of electricity generated by fossil fuels"; unit: "%"; sources: Ember – Yearly Electricity Data Europe (2026); Ember – Yearly Electricity Data (2026); Energy Institute – Statistical Review of World Energy (2026); Pinto et al. – Global historical electricity (2023); Department for Energy Security and Net Zero of the UK – UK electricity capacity and generation by fuel between 1920 and 2020 (2023).

Rows with a blank iso_code are matched by their "country" name: Kosovo -> XKX; regions, income groups and source-defined aggregates (e.g. "Europe (EI)", "G20 (Ember)", "World") and former states are skipped. A blank cell is kept as missing, never 0.
caveats: Share of fuel burned, not of fuel imported: a coal or gas producer (e.g. the US) can have a high fossil share and no import dependence.

scoring.rationale: Shows how much power relies on fuel, not where the fuel comes from; it is the upper limit of the imported-fuel part of the exposure.
